<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Appendix B <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Proofs &amp; Comments</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">B.1</span> Set Theory Foundations (§<a class="dg-xref" href="../vector-spaces/foundations-sets-maps.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Foundations_Sets_Maps">2.1</a>)</h1></header>
<p>This appendix expands on the brief remark made in Section <a class="dg-xref" href="../vector-spaces/foundations-sets-maps.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Foundations_Sets_Maps">2.1</a> regarding the set-theoretic foundations underlying the definitions of sets, maps, and algebraic structures. It summarizes the role of axiomatic set theory—particularly the Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with the Axiom of Choice (ZFC)—as the formal foundation upon which modern mathematics, including the material in these notes, is built.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>Formally, the notions of <em>set</em>, <em>element</em>, <em>subset</em>, <em>intersection</em>, <em>union</em>, and related concepts are rigorously grounded in axiomatic set theory. The most commonly used framework is <strong>Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with the Axiom of Choice</strong> (abbreviated ZFC). This system provides a widely accepted foundation for modern mathematics, resolving classical paradoxes such as Russell’s paradox and enabling the construction of virtually all mathematical objects encountered in fields like analysis, topology, and geometry.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>The <strong>Axiom of Choice</strong> (AC) plays a subtle but significant role within this framework. It is indispensable for certain results—such as Tychonoff’s theorem in topology, or the fact that every vector space admits a basis—but it also leads to counterintuitive consequences, including the existence of non-measurable sets and the Banach-Tarski paradox. Despite this, the use of AC is standard in most of pure mathematics, including the framework employed throughout these notes.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>It is worth noting that ZFC is not the only possible foundation for mathematics. Some branches explore alternatives such as ZF without Choice, category-theoretic frameworks like Elementary Topos Theory, or type-theoretic foundations like Homotopy Type Theory (HoTT). These frameworks differ in how they treat objects, collections, and logical inference, sometimes avoiding certain pathologies at the cost of restricting other constructions.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>Nevertheless, for the purposes of these notes, we adopt a pragmatic approach based on the standard ZFC framework: sets are well-defined collections of elements, and all operations we employ are assumed to be well-behaved within this context.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>A deep exploration of the logical and philosophical foundations of mathematics—including formal logic, model theory, and metamathematics—is essential in its own right but lies beyond the scope of this text. We must start somewhere.</p>
